messages.subject_clean: [BioGeoBEARS] Citation fossil hooks?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Torsten -- I don't think there is a journal publication, but one of these might work:

Matzke, Nicholas J (2013). "Probabilistic Historical Biogeography: New Models for Founder-Event Speciation, Imperfect Detection, and Fossils Allow Improved Accuracy and Model-Testing." Ph.D. Thesis, U.C. Berkeley Department of Integrative BIology.
Proquest: http://search.proquest.com/docview/1526024556

Matzke, Nicholas J; Säilä, Laura (2017). Phylogenetic biogeography of fossil Canidae: combining models of imperfect detection, fossil databases as taphonomic controls, and Biogeographical Stochastic Mapping. Evolution 2017, Portland, Oregon. June 23-27, 2017. http://www.evolutionmeetings.org/evolution-2017---portland-oregon.html YouTube video at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Of6MTpYYzsM

...or the BioGeoBEARS package itself.

However, the "hooks" idea turns out to be basically same as the "sampled ancestor" concept in birth-death-serial-sampling trees with fossils, in that the postulated direct ancestor is represented as a side-branch in the newick tree structure, just with a branchlength of 0.0 (in BEAST2) or <0.00000001 (or whatever you set in BioGeoBEARS).

How these short/zero-length branches are interpreted for a particular model all depends on the programmer. In Lagrange, all branches are extended up to the present to make the tree ultrametric. In BioGeoBEARS, the original branchlengths are used, except for those very short "hooks", which the program interprets as direct ancestors, rather than cladogenesis events.

Cheers,
Nick

messages.body_plain:
Hi Joel,

My gut instinct is:

* If anything, more data (more species) should reduce the number of required optimization steps, because more data = a more peaked likelihood surface = easier optimization

* However, more species will slow down each individual likelihood calculation, although this is only a linear problem (double the species, double the time)

* Adding areas of course dramatically increases the calculation time (worse than quadratic)

* The different optimizers in R have different typical behaviors. For a 2-parameter problem (e.g. classic DEC), typically I recall seeing:

optim: 50-100 steps for optimization
optimx: 50-100 steps (but maybe a bit more than optim)
GenSA: perhaps 2x to 5x more steps

For all of these, each additional free parameter will likely ~double the number of steps required. But GenSA may have some minimum number of steps, it is Generalized Simulated Annealing, basically this is repeating the search again and again at different "temperatures", allowing bigger or smaller jumps between parameter guesses.  For large parameter spaces, GenSA is supposed to be better, and I think this seems to be typically true at even ~5-7 parameters, however someone did once post a case where GenSA in a 2-parameter problem never found an improvement beyond the starting d=0.01, e=0.01, whereas optimx rapidly found a better solution.

Beyond that, I don't know too much about how these work, these are all "off the shelf" optimizers available in base R (optim) or R packages (optimx, GenSA).

Cheers,
Nick

Hi! Apologies this is confusing, I've never gotten a chance to document it all properly.

Dear Joel,

Cladogenetic events happen exactly *at* the speciation event (the node), and can be either sympatry (each descendant inherits the same range as the ancestor), vicariance (each descendant inherits part of the range of the ancestor; can be narrow or wide vicariance), subset sympatry (one of the descendants inherits a single area from the ancestor's range, while the other inherits exactly the same range as the ancestor) or founder-event speciation (one of the descendants inherits the same range as the ancestor, while the other descendant "moves" to a single area that is not contained in the ancestor's range).

Anagenetic events (any number of dispersals or extinctions) occur along the branchs. So you can easily have a cladogenetic event (at the node) followed by an anagenetic event (along the branch). When you look at a BioGeoBEARS output figure, you will notice that there are probabilities of ranges at the bottom of a branch, by the sides of the node. This is the probability of the range occupied by the descendants, immediately after the cladogenetic event. On the other hand, you have probabilities at the top of the branch. In the example below, you have a dispersal event (A >AB) followed by a vicariant event (ancestor: AB > descendant 1: A + descendent 2: B), followed by a dispersal event (B > BC in descendant 2).

                                 A  ------------------------ A
               (A > AB)      |
        A ----------------- AB
                                  |           (B > BC)
                                  B  ----------------------- BC
                           (probability                     (probability at the
                            immediately                     end of the branch)
                            after cladogenetic
                             event)

So, to sum up,  it is not contradictory. Each node can have both cladogenetic events and anagenetic events associated (the former happens at the node itself, the latter happens along the branch that immediately precedes the node). I don't exactly recall the output for BSM tables, but I think that for the example above, it would show both a cladogenetic event (AB > A + B) and an anagenetic event (A > AB) for the same node.

Best,
Ivan
